report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p≥0.192", "p>0.05", "p>0.05", 
"p>0.05"), Text = c("For MRI modality, T2 weighted image (T2WI) showed higher sensitivity (0.745) than T2WI plus diffusion weighted image (DWI) (0.697), while T2WI+DWI had higher specificity (0.809 vs 0.737) and AUC (0.829 vs 0.796), with no significant subgroup differences (p≥0.192).", 
"These differences in sensitivity between DL, ML, and LR were not statistically significant (all p>0.05).", 
"Logistic regression showed significantly higher pooled specificity than ML (p=0.030), whereas the differences between DL and ML and between DL and LR were not statistically significant (p>0.05).", 
"None of the pairwise differences in sensitivity or specificity between DL, ML, and LR within this combined category were statistically significant (all p>0.05)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Background: In rectal cancer (RC), tumor deposits (TDs) are clinically important as they are associated with a negative impact on prognosis and affect risk stratification as well as management plans.
MRI radiomics combined with artificial intelligence (AI) has been explored for non-invasive preoperative TDs detection.
However, results vary across studies; therefore, we performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to pool their diagnostic test accuracy (DTA).

Methods: This systematic review and DTA meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Diagnostic Test Accuracy and reported in adherence to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses of Diagnostic Test Accuracy Studies (PRISMA-DTA).
Databases were screened for DTA studies of MRI-based radiomics predicting TDs in adult RC patients with histopathology as reference.
Results: Nine studies (2589 patients) were identified.

Across included studies, the bivariate metaanalysis showed pooled sensitivity of 0.765 (95% CI 0.714 -0.809) and specificity of 0.790 (95% CI 0.750 -0.825), with overall AUC of 0.845 and very low heterogeneity (I² = 7.3%).
In validation datasets, diagnostic performance remained consistent (AUC 0.806), with pooled sensitivity 0.751 (95% CI 0.681 -0.809) and specificity 0.751 (95% CI 0.681 -0.809).

For MRI modality, T2 weighted image (T2WI) showed higher sensitivity (0.745) than T2WI plus diffusion weighted image (DWI) (0.697), while T2WI+DWI had higher specificity (0.809 vs 0.737) and AUC (0.829 vs 0.796), with no significant subgroup differences (p≥0.192).
Models combining radiomics with clinical/radiological variables achieved significantly higher sensitivity (0.842 vs 0.657, p<0.001) and higher AUC (0.827 vs 0.752), with comparable specificity.

text.text: Conclusion: MRI-based radiomics demonstrates good accuracy for preoperative detection of tumor deposits in RC.
The integration of radiomics with clinical or imaging features increases the accuracy of identification.
Amongst the MRI modalities, models that utilize the combination of T2WI plus DWI are more accurate than those using T2WI or DWI only.
The trends in mortality rates emerged as a better indicator of cancer prognosis rather than incidence or survival which might be affected by screen-detection biases.

text.text: Radiomics has emerged as a promising tool which can aid in diagnosis and prognosis of malignancy.

It is a risk-free tool capable of extracting and analyzing quantitative features that cannot be captured by the naked eye from conventional medical images through machine learning and artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms, resulting in signatures reflecting tumor phenotype 14.
text.formatted: It is a risk-free tool capable of extracting and analyzing quantitative features that cannot be captured by the naked eye from conventional medical images through machine learning and artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms, resulting in signatures reflecting tumor phenotype <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref>.

text.text: Recently, several studies have developed radiomic models incorporating preoperative pelvic MRI to predict TDs in RC patients, resulting in better prediction of TDs.
Despite the promising role, the field requires advances to establish optimal feature selection and ideal algorithms.

So, in this study, we conduct a systematic review and diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) meta-analysis collating all eligible studies and pooling the paired sensitivity and specificity using a bivariate random-effects model.

By isolating workflows that remain accurate across diverse settings, our analysis offers a practical, reproducible radiomics roadmap for routine pre-operative staging of tumor deposits and more informed treatment decisions.
We conducted this systematic review and DTA meta-analysis in accordance with the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Diagnostic Test Accuracy 15 .

text.text: In-depth literature search went through PubMed, the Cochrane Library, SCOPUS, and Web of Science databases.

A systematic literature search was employed using these keywords [("rectal neoplasms" OR "rectal cancer" OR "rectal carcinoma" OR "rectal neoplasm*") AND ("magnetic resonance imaging" OR "MRI" OR "MR imaging" OR "magnetic resonance") AND (radiomic* OR "radiomics" OR "texture analysis" OR "feature extraction") up to July 2025 with no limitations or filters to ensure no studies are missed.
The choice of broad search terms was a pragmatic decision to include as many studies as possible.
Studies were deemed eligible for inclusion if all the following criteria were met: Population: Adult patients with histologically confirmed RC who underwent preoperative pelvic MRI.
Index test: MRI-based radiomics features analyzed using AI to detect the presence of TDs.
Reference test: Histopathological assessment of resected specimens as the reference standard for confirming the presence or absence of TDs.

Study Design: Studies of DTA with prospective and retrospective designs including sufficient data to form a 2×2 contingency table; true positives, false positives, false negatives, and true negatives.

Outcome Measures: Reported or permitted the calculation of accuracy metrics including sensitivity and specificity, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), or other relevant measures.

Studies were excluded if: 1) the index model did not incorporate MRI-based radiomics or MRIderived image features (for example, models based solely on clinical variables or on non-MRI imaging modalities such as CT or PET); 2) if the reference standard for TDs was not histopathology of the surgical specimen; 3) if they did not report or did not allow derivation of essential diagnostic accuracy data (including AUC, sensitivity, specificity, or the cell counts required to compute true positives, false positives, false negatives, and true negatives); 4) non-original publications such as reviews, conference abstracts without full data, editorials, letters, expert opinions; 5) special design such as animal studies, phantom studies, and purely technical feasibility studies that did not provide patient-level diagnostic accuracy data; or 6) articles not available in English language.

text.text: In subgroup analysis of pooled DTA, T2WI alone showed pooled sensitivity of 0.745 (95% CI: 0.625-0.837), compared with 0.697 (95% CI: 0.527-0.825) for combined T2WI+DWI.

The pooled area under the curve (AUC) was slightly higher for T2WI+DWI (0.829) than for T2WI alone (0.796), suggesting a modest improvement in overall discriminatory performance with multisequence input.

text.text: Despite promising data reported with high performance metrics such as sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and AUC, however, several challenges stand against implementation such as small sample dataset, algorithm generalizability, and integration in clinical practice 44.
text.formatted: Despite promising data reported with high performance metrics such as sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and AUC, however, several challenges stand against implementation such as small sample dataset, algorithm generalizability, and integration in clinical practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">44</ref>.

text.text: To the best of our knowledge this study is the first DTA meta-analysis studying the role of MRI-based radiomics in prediction of TDs in RC patients.
In this study, MRI-based radiomics models demonstrate reliable detection of TDs in RC, with reproducible discrimination across included studies which are largely persisting in validation subsets.
These findings are clinically relevant, given the high ambiguity of tumor deposits with small nodes, vessels, fibrosis, and postinflammatory changes.
The delineation of subgroups affords clinical insight.

First, expanding the image data input from high-resolution T2WI to include DWI did not result in consistent improvement in TDs detection, reinforcing the notion that TDs detection is not primarily limited by the visibility of TDs on one of the two sequences, but rather by the ambiguity of the TDs and other similar structures and the inherent uncertainty.

This aligns with contemporary rectal MRI practice, where high-quality T2WI remains an essential component for initial RC detection and staging, while DWI is used only when the image quality and interpretative context support its inclusion 45.
text.formatted: This aligns with contemporary rectal MRI practice, where high-quality T2WI remains an essential component for initial RC detection and staging, while DWI is used only when the image quality and interpretative context support its inclusion <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">45</ref>.

text.text: Second and most consequential for clinical translation the models that combine radiomics with clinical/radiological parameters seem to have achieved significantly better case detection with no commensurate increase in false positive detection.

This is biologically understandable, as the TDs detection probability is heavily dependent on tumor phenotype and staging context (e.g., extramural spread, vascular invasion proxies, mesorectal risk) features that are not captured by texture alone.

Overall, a deployment-ready TDs model should be context-fused by design (radiomics plus structured radiological/clinical predictors), built on high-resolution oblique axial T2W MRI as mandatory core input, with DWI/ADC included as an optional auxiliary stream primarily to stabilize specificity, using IBSI-standardized feature extraction and transparent reporting 46, 47.
text.formatted: Overall, a deployment-ready TDs model should be context-fused by design (radiomics plus structured radiological/clinical predictors), built on high-resolution oblique axial T2W MRI as mandatory core input, with DWI/ADC included as an optional auxiliary stream primarily to stabilize specificity, using IBSI-standardized feature extraction and transparent reporting <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">46,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">47</ref>.

text.text: The fact that no consistent "winner" tends to emerge across algorithm families once clinical/radiological context is factored in supports a core assumption for TDs detection, model formulation and validation approach take precedence over classifier choice.

This reinforces the findings from clinical prediction studies, where apparent improvements from machine learning over logistic regression often diminish in value in pragmatic validation and full disclosure 48.
text.formatted: This reinforces the findings from clinical prediction studies, where apparent improvements from machine learning over logistic regression often diminish in value in pragmatic validation and full disclosure <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">48</ref>.

text.text: The recurrent signal of high sensitivity with deep learning should also be considered.

A possible explanation is that DL feature learning can capture structured/contextual information, such as irregularities in nodules, patterns at the mesorectal invasion, and relationships to the primary tumor, which radiomic features may lose through their handcrafted process, thereby aiding in case-finding 49.
text.formatted: A possible explanation is that DL feature learning can capture structured/contextual information, such as irregularities in nodules, patterns at the mesorectal invasion, and relationships to the primary tumor, which radiomic features may lose through their handcrafted process, thereby aiding in case-finding <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">49</ref>.

text.text: The opposite argument is that sensitivity is the metric most susceptible to class imbalance, threshold selection, and domain shift.

DL models, especially in data-limited, single-or few-center settings typical of TD datasets, are prone to shortcut learning and calibration drift, leading to 'optimistic' sensitivity that does not generalize 50 .
text.formatted: DL models, especially in data-limited, single-or few-center settings typical of TD datasets, are prone to shortcut learning and calibration drift, leading to 'optimistic' sensitivity that does not generalize <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">50</ref> .

text.text: Thus, if the intended clinical role is "flagging" (maximizing detection), DL is a justifiable contender only in the context of a multimodal fusion framework and only post locked-threshold external validation plus calibration and workflow assessments; if not, then regularized regression or gradient-boosted models based on fused radiomics plus structured predictors may provide similar discrimination with better stability and interpretability, and will be more readily implementable in the near-term.
Although the results remain encouraging, certain limitations and considerations need to be noted.
The first being that the number of studies is still small, and all the studies being examined are from China.
This limits the generalizability of the findings to other countries and health care systems.

Secondly, as most studies are single-center, retrospective studies, they are more prone to selection bias and may exhibit greater model performance inappropriately, compared to prospective multicenter studies.
The third consideration is the lack of uniformity across studies in MRI acquisition, segmentation, radiomic feature extraction software, and modeling methodologies.
This could compromise the stability and reproducibility of the features.
The fourth limitation is that several studies relied on internal validation, which most likely limited their external validation.
This could potentially lead to great overestimates of the study's diagnostic inconsistency.
Lastly, the reports on the studies of different AI systems and sandwiches were inconsistent and not standardized.
Therefore, the need for more studies is great in the area of utilizing high-grade, validated radiomics, multicenter, prospective studies in greater numbers.
Future research should prioritize large multicenter prospective studies to improve the generalizability and clinical reliability of AI-based MRI radiomics models for tumor deposit detection.

Standardization of imaging acquisition parameters, segmentation methods, and radiomics feature extraction-such as adherence to the Image Biomarker Standardisation Initiative (IBSI) framework-will be important for improving reproducibility across institutions 51 .
text.formatted: Standardization of imaging acquisition parameters, segmentation methods, and radiomics feature extraction-such as adherence to the Image Biomarker Standardisation Initiative (IBSI) framework-will be important for improving reproducibility across institutions <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">51</ref> .

text.text: Moreover, future models should integrate radiomic features with clinical, pathological, and conventional imaging variables, as multimodal approaches may better capture tumor biology and improve predictive performance.

Finally, rigorous external validation and clinical impact studies are needed to determine whether these models can meaningfully improve preoperative staging and support treatment decision-making in routine clinical practice.

MRI-based radiomics shows good performance for the preoperative identification of tumor deposits in rectal cancer, exhibiting consistent sensitivity and specificity across all studies and validation datasets.
Case detection is enhanced when radiomics is integrated with other clinical or radiological elements compared to radiomics in isolation, demonstrating the value of multimodal prediction approaches.

Although high-resolution T2-weighted MRI primarily maintains the fundamental imaging input, the addition of diffusion-weighted imaging mildly increases specificity and overall discriminating performance.

In conclusion, although AI-based MRI radiomics provides a promising non-invasive method for preoperative risk stratification and rectal cancer treatment planning, wider external validation and standardized radiomics procedures are critical for clinical use.
